hints: A Type I error means rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_0$ is actually true. Say what $\text{H}_0$ claims about $\mu$ and the gym times, then what the management would wrongly conclude.
walkthrough:
**What a Type I error is**

In a hypothesis test we can make two kinds of mistake. A **Type I error** is rejecting the null hypothesis $\text{H}_0$ when it is in fact true. (A Type II error is the opposite: not rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when it is false.)

**Put it in this context**

Here $\text{H}_0$ says the mean time is still $42.4$ minutes, that the new equipment has made no difference. So a Type I error is: the test leads the management to conclude that the mean time has changed (is no longer 42.4), when in fact $\mu$ is still 42.4.

**Final answer**

A Type I error is concluding that the (population) mean time has changed, or is not $42.4$ minutes, when in fact $\mu$ has not changed and is still $42.4$.

hints: Look at the management's wording ('has changed'): does it name a direction? Decide whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed, then write $\text{H}_0$ and $\text{H}_1$ about $\mu$ yourself, saying what $\mu$ stands for.

The sample mean of 20 customers has the distribution $\text{N}\left(42.4, \dfrac{38.2}{20}\right)$ under $\text{H}_0$. Standardise: $z = \dfrac{45.6 - 42.4}{\sqrt{38.2 \div 20}}$ — the 20 must appear.
Work in this order on your calculator: divide 38.2 by 20, take the square root, then divide $45.6 - 42.4$ by that. Give $z$ to 3 decimal places.

Two-tailed at 2.5% means half of the 2.5% in each tail. Find the critical $z$ for that upper-tail area from the normal table, and compare your $z$ with it (or compare a tail probability with half of 2.5%).

Is your $z$ bigger than the critical value, that is, in the rejection region? Write the conclusion about $\mu$ in context, in non-definite words ('there is evidence that…' or 'there is no evidence that…'), not 'proved'.
walkthrough:
**Hypotheses (B1)**

The management wants to know whether $\mu$ has **changed**, not whether it has gone up or down. So the test is two-tailed.

$$\text{H}_0: \mu = 42.4$$

$$\text{H}_1: \mu \neq 42.4$$

Here $\mu$ is the population mean time (in minutes) spent by customers at the gym. Writing just 'mean' is not enough; name the population mean or $\mu$.

**Distribution of the sample mean**

The times are $\text{N}(\mu, 38.2)$, where 38.2 is the **variance**. If $\text{H}_0$ is true, the mean $\bar{X}$ of a sample of $n = 20$ has variance $\dfrac{38.2}{20}$ (an average varies less than single values):

$$\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(42.4, \frac{38.2}{20}\right)$$

The population is normal, so $\bar{X}$ is exactly normal, with no approximation needed.

**Standardise (M1)**

$$z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 / n}} = \frac{45.6 - 42.4}{\sqrt{38.2 \div 20}}$$

The scheme insists that the 20 appears: you divide by $n$ because it is a mean of 20 customers. A very common slip is to use $\sqrt{38.2}$ alone.

One step at a time:

$$45.6 - 42.4 = 3.2$$

$$38.2 \div 20 = 1.91 \qquad \sqrt{1.91} = 1.3820\ldots$$

$$z = \frac{3.2}{1.3820\ldots} = 2.315$$

This earns the A1: $z = 2.315$ (the scheme writes $\pm$ because either sign is accepted for a two-tailed test).

**Find the critical value**

The significance level is 2.5% and the test is two-tailed, so we put $1.25\%$ in each tail. The upper-tail critical value is the $z$ with $\Phi(z) = 1 - 0.0125$, which is $0.9875$. Using the normal table (or the inverse normal on your calculator):

$$z_{\text{crit}} = 2.240 \text{ (the table value; the exact value is } 2.2414\text{, and the scheme accepts 2.241)}$$

**Compare (M1)**

Is our $z$ beyond the critical value?

$$2.315 > 2.240$$

Yes, so our $z$ lies in the rejection region. Alternative: $\text{P}(Z > 2.315) = 1 - \Phi(2.315) = 0.0103$, and since $0.0103 < 0.0125$, we reach the same conclusion. (Or two tails: $2 \times 0.0103 = 0.0206 < 0.025$.)

**Conclusion in context (A1 FT)**

We reject $\text{H}_0$. There is evidence, at the 2.5% significance level, that the mean time spent by customers at the gym has changed from $42.4$ minutes.

Keep the wording non-definite ('there is evidence that…'), because the test shows we have enough evidence, not certainty.

**Final answer**

$z = 2.315$ (3 d.p.), which exceeds the critical value $2.240$ (that is, $2.240 < 2.315$). Reject $\text{H}_0$: there is evidence that the mean time $\mu$ has changed from $42.4$ minutes.
